films.w: Australian mockumentary about a family haunted after their teenage daughter drowns. The closest match to Late Night with the Devil’s fake-documentary feel, built on slow dread.
A horror livestream crew goes into a notorious abandoned Korean asylum to chase views. If you love REC, start here.
British friends hold a séance over Zoom during lockdown. 56 minutes, no filler, properly jumpy.
Starts minutes after REC ends, in the same building, through SWAT helmet cameras. A must since you loved the first.
Vatican investigators set up cameras in a West Country church. The tunnel finale is pure As Above, So Below.
A student crew films a woman with Alzheimer’s for a documentary. It isn’t Alzheimer’s. Contains one of found footage’s best images.
Taiwanese cursed-video mockumentary that eventually turns the camera on you. Folk religion and real dread.
Thai mockumentary following a village shaman whose niece starts changing. Slow first half, then a genuinely unhinged final act.
A Halloween haunted-house attraction’s opening night ends in disaster. Clown mannequins that keep turning up somewhere new.
One night in Manhattan, filmed on a party camcorder, as something enormous arrives. Still holds up.
A commuter is stuck looping an endless subway corridor. Spot an anomaly and turn back, or start again. The closest film to Backrooms.
A dinner party, a passing comet and realities that start to overlap. A micro-budget mind-bender for Vivarium fans.
Two brothers go back to the UFO cult they escaped as kids. Time loops and cosmic dread.
Shipwrecked friends board a deserted ocean liner. A clever time-loop puzzle box.
A grandmother’s dementia turns her house into an endless, rotting maze. Devastating final scene.
From The Ritual’s director. A widow finds plans for a mirror-image house. Brilliant impossible-space scares.
A vertical prison where one food platform descends through hundreds of floors. Cube with teeth.
Wildcard. Two kids, a house whose doors disappear, near-total darkness. The most liminal film there is and the most divisive. Skip it if Backrooms felt too vague.
An Irish trawler snags something that gets into the water supply. Quarantine paranoia, basically The Thing at sea.
1983. A Soviet cosmonaut comes home with a passenger living inside him. Alien meets Cold War period piece.
A deep-sea drilling station collapses and something ancient is down there with the survivors. Critics shrugged; Alien fans tend not to.
Lovecraft, Nicolas Cage and a meteorite that mutates a farm and everyone on it. Cosmic body horror in The Void’s lane.
After a fall into a cave, a couple’s bodies start fusing. Relationship drama played as The Thing.
A double-booked Airbnb, then the basement. Go in knowing nothing else.
Jordan Peele’s creature feature in the sky above a horse ranch. Big, eerie and original.
A near-wordless alien home invasion with genuinely creepy visitors. A tight 90 minutes.
An International Space Station crew wakes a Martian organism. An unashamed Alien homage, done well.

films.t: The Last Voyage of the Demeter
films.w: Dracula as the xenomorph, on one cargo ship from Carpathia to London. Period creature horror for Nosferatu fans.
A Korean village, a stranger, a shaman and a spreading sickness. Long, and a masterpiece.
1932 Mississippi. Twin brothers open a juke joint and vampires come knocking. Period piece and creature feature in one.
New from Damian Mc Carthy, who made Caveat and Oddity. A novelist at a remote inn hears about a witch haunting the honeymoon suite.
Siblings return to their dying father’s isolated farm. The bleakest possession film in years.
1988 Tehran during the air raids. A djinn haunts a mother and daughter trapped in their flat.
1905, a cult on a remote Welsh island. Wicker Man energy with one truly brutal scene.
1971 Rome, a young nun and a convent conspiracy. Gorgeous 70s period horror.
A devout palliative nurse in Scarborough decides she’s on a mission. Slow-burn, with an unforgettable last shot.
1985. A British film censor during the video-nasty panic starts losing the line between film and life. Period horror soaked in VHS.
Hugh Grant traps two young missionaries in a house that keeps going down. Claustrophobic and clever.
A 90s FBI agent on a satanic murder case. Oppressive atmosphere and an unrecognisable Nicolas Cage.
South Sudanese refugees are housed in an English council house that doesn’t want them.
Guillermo del Toro’s gothic creature epic. More beautiful than scary, for the same craft you liked in Nosferatu.
A gamer is trapped in his Seoul flat as an outbreak hits. The Night Eats the World, Korean-style.
An outbreak breaks out on a bullet train. Still the modern benchmark.
Danny Boyle and Alex Garland return to infected Britain with a folk-horror streak and a few brutal moments.

films.t: The Girl with All the Gifts
films.w: A British fungal apocalypse seen through one very unusual child. Smart and bleak.
Bunker paranoia with a terrifying John Goodman. Tight as a drum.
From Trollhunter’s director. One night in a morgue basement with an impossible corpse.
An island house, a man in a chained harness, a rabbit with a drum. Irish and deeply creepy.
A blind psychic, a wooden mannequin and a murder in rural Ireland. The best Irish horror in years.
Seventeen kids from one class vanish at 2:17am. Barbarian’s director doing an ensemble mystery.
Australian teenagers get possessed for kicks using an embalmed hand.
A British anthology with Martin Freeman and Paul Whitehouse. Twisty, creepy and fun.
Cronenberg’s companion piece to The Thing. The practical effects are still elite.
The BBC’s fake live Halloween broadcast that panicked the country. Late Night with the Devil’s direct ancestor.
A rescue crew boards a ship that went somewhere and came back. Critics hated it; Alien fans love it.
Barry Levinson’s found-footage eco-outbreak in a Maryland bay town on the Fourth of July. Parasites, panic and a REC-style escalation.
A ghost-hunting show locks itself in an asylum overnight and the corridors stop leading where they should. Found footage turning liminal.
A couple and a carjacker trapped in a petrol station by a parasite that rebuilds bodies. Low-budget, practical, very The Thing.
Benson and Moorhead’s first: a man handcuffs his addict friend in a cabin and someone keeps leaving them recordings. The Endless’s prequel, of sorts.
A paranormal researcher’s last documentary, pieced together from fake TV segments. Japan’s found-footage masterpiece.
A videographer answers an online ad from a man who wants his day filmed. Two actors, one camera, growing unease.
Picks up straight after The Descent as a rescue team goes back down. Weaker than the first, still pitch-black and grim.
Two crew members wake on a silent colony ship with no memory, and they aren’t alone. Event Horizon meets The Descent.
Danny Boyle’s crew flying a bomb into the dying sun. Hard sci-fi that turns into space horror in its last act.
Ben Wheatley’s lockdown folk horror: scientists hike into a forest where something talks through the trees. Strobe-heavy and nasty in places.
Two hitmen take a job that drifts into something very old and very English. Brutal and bleak: The Wicker Man by way of a crime film.
A devout police sergeant flies to a Hebridean island to find a missing girl. The folk-horror original and Midsommar’s grandfather.
A soon-to-be stepmother snowed in with two kids at a remote lodge as her cult past catches up. Cold, claustrophobic, bleak.
A disgraced YouTuber livestreams a night in a haunted house. Found footage played for laughs and scares in equal measure.
A taped-off-TV 1987 local news special that goes very wrong, adverts and all. Late Night with the Devil’s scrappier cousin.
Found-footage anthology framed by a SWAT raid. The strongest V/H/S, though one segment goes properly gory.
Kiyoshi Kurosawa’s ghosts leaking through the internet into an emptying Tokyo. The most liminal pre-Backrooms film there is.
A family moves into a cottage by an Irish forest the locals say belongs to something else. Practical-effects creature folk horror.
A grieving mother and an occultist seal themselves in a remote Welsh house for a months-long ritual. Claustrophobic, patient, then unforgettable.
An ex-cop chasing a missing teenager stumbles into a cult and something cosmic. Long, strange and a genuine cult favourite.
A journalist hunting her missing friend digs into CIA drug tests and a numbers-station broadcast. Found-footage cosmic horror.
A teenager performs a ritual to curse her mother after a move to the woods, and something answers. Small, mean and effective.
A Dublin teenager’s mother comes back from a disappearance not quite herself, just before Halloween. Irish folk horror.
Two girls left at a Catholic boarding school over winter break. Oz Perkins before Longlegs: slow, cold, then vicious.
A curse passed on by sex and a slow walking figure only you can see. Brilliant synth score and long, patient frames.
1970s Yorkshire: a grieving couple, a cursed field and an old tree. Quiet British folk horror.
Fifty strangers wake in a dark room and vote every two minutes on who dies. Cube as a parlour game.
Rural Argentina, where possession spreads like rabies and the rules for containing it are breaking down. The Crazies meets The Wailing. Superb, but cruel to kids and animals with no warning.
From the Talk to Me directors: two foster kids, a grieving foster mum and a ritual. Brilliant and genuinely nasty; one scene of self-injury is the hardest watch of last year.
A breeding venomous spider loose in a Paris tower block under quarantine. REC with spiders. Only go in if spiders on screen don’t bother you.
A Taipei outbreak where the infected turn gleefully sadistic. Expertly made, but the violence, including sexual violence, is the point. The closest thing here to Hostel.
Art the Clown stalks two women through a Halloween night. A gore showcase with a thin film around it.
Bigger, longer, nastier. Famous for audience walkouts; the kills are the whole show.
Art the Clown at Christmas. More of the same splatter, if 2 didn’t put you off.
A slow-burn western rescue mission into cannibal country. Excellent for 100 minutes, then one infamously brutal scene that’s pure Hostel territory.
Irish-language folk horror: a carer is sent to a remote village to look after a recluse who swears the ‘good people’ took her decades ago. Starve Acre-style dread with real Irish folklore under it.

Argentine haunting where paranormal investigators descend on a Buenos Aires street plagued by impossible events. From the When Evil Lurks director, and some of the best jump scares of the last decade.
Canadian mockumentary: a crew digs into a boy who vanished filming in the Vancouver Island woods in 2001. A Blair Witch homage that turns properly nasty in its final act. On Shudder from 31 October.
A medical mission deep in the Amazon is hunted by a colossal serpent worshipped as a god. Festival crowds called it the bloodiest, scariest giant-snake film yet; jungle-predator energy for Prey fans.

films.t: Hell House LLC Origins: The Carmichael Manor
films.w: A couple film themselves staying at a manor linked to an unsolved family massacre. The strongest Hell House sequel, with the series’ trademark static figures that move when you look away.

films.aka: Errementari: The Blacksmith and the Devil
films.w: Basque dark fairy tale set in 1843: an investigator tracks a reclusive blacksmith who keeps a demon caged in his forge. Period folk horror with great practical creature work; on Netflix.
Indonesian folk horror from Joko Anwar: a woman returns to her ancestral village to claim an inheritance and finds a curse that has children born without skin. Midsommar-grade village dread.
Mexican body horror about an expectant mother stalked by a contorted, bone-cracking figure from folklore. The sound design alone will get under your skin.
South London teens defend their tower block from an alien invasion on Bonfire Night. Fast, funny creature feature with brilliantly simple practical monsters; free on Channel 4.
